title: Outcome Bias
description: We judge the quality of a decision based on how it turned out, rather than on the information and reasoning available at the time. A good outcome makes a bad decision look smart; a bad outcome makes a good decision look foolish.
shortDescription: We judge the quality of a decision based on how it turned out, rather than on the information and reasoning available at the time. A good outcome makes a bad decision look smart; a bad outcome makes a good decision look foolish.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: We judge the quality of a decision based on how it turned out, rather than on the information and reasoning available at the time. A good outcome makes a bad decision look smart; a bad outcome makes a good decision look foolish.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: A gambler who wins a bet on a horse is praised for his “insight,” even though he picked randomly.
A CEO’s reckless expansion that luckily succeeds is celebrated as “visionary.” A careful decision that fails due to an unforeseeable event gets the manager fired.
After a successful surgery despite poor technique, the surgeon is hailed as brilliant; the next patient dies from the same poor technique.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Evaluating past decisions solely by results.
Rewarding people for lucky wins and punishing them for unlucky losses.
Forgetting to examine the decision‑making process.

sections.title: Real Phrases
content: “He must know what he’s doing; look at his track record.”

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: You feel a decision was obviously correct because things went well.
You can’t describe what the person knew at the time; you only know what happened later.
Success leads you to skip the post‑mortem.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: The outcome is vivid and tangible; the counterfactual is abstract. The brain prefers a simple story: good result = good decision.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: When evaluating a decision, reconstruct what was known at the time. Ask: “Given that information, was this a reasonable bet?”
In organizations, separate performance evaluation from decision quality reviews.
Use pre‑mortems: before the outcome is known, define what would make the decision a good or bad one.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Dismissing process because “results are all that matter.” A bad process will eventually produce bad results.
Judging your own past decisions too harshly because of bad luck rather than bad thinking.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A junior trader makes a huge, unauthorized bet and gets lucky. The bank promotes him. A year later, he repeats the same reckless behavior and loses billions. The earlier outcome bias created a hero, then a villain.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: Outcomes lie. A good result can wear a stupid decision like a fancy suit. Examine the process, not just the profit.
